This form must be executed in duplicate when a child is transferred from a reservation to a nonreservation school. The Superintendent of the nonreservation school will retain the original for his files, and the duplicate shall be deposited in the Agency records. The agent will then send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate as provided by law. All the blanks must be properly filled in every case. If the information called for on any part of the blank is not known, that fact should be stated. No space should be left unfilled. Whether the parent is living or dead, their names must be given. The person who signs the blank as consenting to the transfer should indicate his relation to the applicant by marking out the word "parent," "guardian," or "next of kin," leaving unmarked only the title appropriate to the signer. INDORSEMENTS. The laws relating to the transfer of Indian children from reservations and schools are as follows: That hereafter no Indian child shall be sent from any Indian reservation to a school beyond the State or Territory in which said reservation is situated without the voluntary consent of the father or mother of such child if either of them are living, and if neither of them are living without the voluntary consent of the next of kin of such child. Such consent shall be made before the agent of the reservation, and he shall send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate that such consent has been voluntarily given before such child shall be removed from such reservation. And it shall be unlawful for any Indian agent or other employee of the Government to induce, or seek to induce, by withholding rations or by other improper means, the parents or next of kin of any Indian to consent to the removal of any Indian child beyond the limits of any reservation. (28 Stats., p. 906.) Provided, That hereafter no Indian child shall be taken from any school in any State or Territory to a school in any other State against its will or without the written consent of its parents. (29 Stats., p. 348.) That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both Superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted. This form is to be used only in transfers from reservations or Indian schools to nonreservation schools. CASE RECORD. Mr. Patsy Moses, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington. Dear Patsy: I am enclosing a U S Treasury check, #2129150 in the sum of $2.12, representing interest on a $100 Liberty Bond. As you will note, Patsy, the check is made payable to Squealk Moses, so I suppose you will see that he uses it for some good purposes. Very truly yours, Fred C. O'Boyle Superintendent. SJ-Encl. Dear Patsy: In reply to your letter of January 24th regarding your money on deposit here, would advise that there is $25.46. It will require only about half of the above amount for you to return to Cushman, and you will have the balance upon your arrival here. Yours very sincerely, Superintendent The money you want of me to come home. That's all I want to find out. Your truly friend, Patsy L. Moses How much? $25.46 Cobville Agency Wespeben, O. Wash. Jan. 1-24-19 Mr. E.H. Hammond Cushman Agency Dear friend: I'm writing to you to let you know I would be very much pleased if you tell how much money I've got left over there. Forty dollars was sent from here last spring to come home on. But I came home too soon. The money got there after I came home. That's all I want to find out. Your truly friend, Patsy L. Moser How much? $25.46 Colville, Agency. Nespelem, Wash. Nov. 3, 1918. E.H. Hammond, Supt. Cushman, Agency. Dear sir; Well I haven't received my desk and chair I don't know what is the matter with them. I wrote to the agent in Almira. I haven't received any answer yet. I don't see why they they don't sent them in. Mr. Hammond how much money have I got left over there? What are you going to do with it? Are you going to sent them over? How is Annie getting along? Tell her not to get lonesome. Tell her to study hard. Your truly friend, Patsy Moses, Mr. Keller This furniture was shipped by express. Can't you trace it for me? Ever Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Nov. 15, 1918. Mr. Patsy Moses, Pespelem, Wash. Dear Patsy: Your desk and chair were shipped you by express during the vacation period as there was no way to prepay charges by freight. If you send the $4.97 at once to A.P. Wilcoxon, the Express Agent, with directions how to ship the goods to you, you will soon receive them. Otherwise they will be returned to Cushman and the expenses will be doubled for you to pay. Sincerely yours, Superintendent Colville Agency Nespelem Sta. Nov. 10, 1918. E.H. Hammond, Sup't Dear Sir: I received this card from the nearest Express station. But I don't understand it. I don't understand how you shipped them over to Almira. I thought it was supposed to be delivered to me. Your truly, Patsy Reproduced at the National Archives at Seattle Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington June 18, 1918. Mr. Fred C. Morgan Nespelem, Washington. Dear Mr. Morgan, Replying to your letter of June 3, 1918: I have looked up Patsy Moses' status and find that he has completed the three year enrollment period and is entitled to receive transportation home, or would be if there were funds available. I have advised Patsy of the impossibility of paying his transportation home until after the funds for 1919 are available if he cares to wait at school so long. The thirty dollars ($30.00) sent by Patsy's father were delivered to Patsy and Annie and both were cautioned that the money was for their transportation home. In spite of this fact, both children proceeded to spend all the money and are in consequence without funds, much to their disgust. It may prove, I hope, a much needed lesson as neither child has a sense of the value of money. Very truly yours, Superintendent DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash. June 3, 1918. Supt. E. H. Hammond, Cushman School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mr. Hammond: I have received your letter of May 27, 1918 inclosing vacation requests for vacations of Colville Indians attending the Cushman School. It is my understanding that Patsy Moses was enrolled for a term of three years and that his term expired at the closing of school this year. If this is correct the vacation request submitted for him will not be signed as the Government will necessarily pay his transportation home. In this connection the father of Patsy and Annie Moses has advised me that he sent $30.00 to his children on which to return home. Please see Patsy and Annie and have them deposit sufficient money with you to insure the return of Annie Moses. I note that you have submitted a request for Theresa Dupuis. This girl is not a Colville allottee and the request is returned herewith. Very truly yours, Fred C. Morgan Superintendent Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Oct. 7, 1918. Mr. Patsy Moses, Nespelem, Wash. Dear Patsy: In reply to your inquiry of September 28th relative to your desk and chair would advise that they were shipped you by express in August. You should call at the nearest express office and get them. You foolish boy! You should not give up school until you have completed the eighth grade work. Hope you will change your mind. Sincerely yours, Superintendent EHH-S Nespelem, Wash. Sept. 28, 1918. E.A. Hammond, Cushman Agency. Dear Sir: I haven't received my desk and chair. I don't know what is the matter. Did you get enough pupils from here? How many pupils did you get from here? I'm sorry to say that I wouldn't be back to school this year. Yours truly friend, Potey Moss Was written to Kelley Lewis Monohon, Wash returned again & again Cushman School Lassona WY May 2, 1918 Hello old sport, How are you getting along? I'm getting along very well. Are you working every day? I heard you was in the saw mill. You know what you are you are damn bone head. I'm here in Cushman. Going to school every day. You damn big bonehead. When are you coming over here. So you have got a Ford. How many cans of Copenhagen do you chew every day? Well I wouldn't tell you very much now. Maybe I could tell you more next time. Your old friend Betty Moore Napelen Wash July 13 1918 Dear sir: I'm going to write you a little to let you know I'm very well. How about that rocking chair and the writing desk. When are you going to send them over? I had a good time here this fourth. I wish you could send them as soon as you can. Your truly friend Patsy Moses Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. August 7, 1918. Mr. Leroy: Dear Sir: Please send by express, two crates - writing desk and chair - now in carpentry shop - addressed to Patsy Moses, Nespelem, Washington. Very respectfully, Superintendent. Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. August 7, 1918 Mr. Patsy Moses, Neapelem, Washington. Dear Patsy: I received your letter asking for your desk and chair and have instructed Mr. LeRoy to ship them to you the first trip he makes to town. I hope you have been enjoying your vacation and will be not only ready, but anxious to return to school September 5th - with a dozen new pupils. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent. 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash. April 22, 1918. Mr. E. H. Hammond, Supt. Cushman School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mr. Hammond: I have to request that Patsy Moses be granted an extension of one week in his leave of absence. His leave would expire today, but I believe he should be allowed one week more so that he will again take up his school work on Monday April 29th. Patsy's father, who is known as Peter Dan or Peter Dan Moses has been dependent on Patsy and his older brother Charles in assisting him in the Spring planting. Charles has been sick and unable to do his share of this work, making Peter Dan dependent on Patsy for all of it. While I regret the necessity for making this request, I believe that the circumstances warrant it and although Peter could use Patsy for a longer period, he has agreed to send him back if the boy is granted one week of additional absence from school. Very truly yours, Fred C. Morgan Superintendent. CUSHMAN INDIAN SCHOOL Tacoma, Washington April 20, 1918 Mr. Patsy Moses Nespelem, Washington Dear Patsy: I just received a letter from Carter in which he tells me that you are pretty sick. I am very sorry to hear it as I was in hopes you would have a pleasant vacation and would be in fine shape to return for the remainder of the school year. The boys and girls seem to be enjoying themselves and have been studying hard. I have been very busy but if your papa will send $2.50 I will have your chair crated and shipped to you. I know "mamma" will be very proud of your work. Get well soon so that you may pass into Grade VII with flying colors. Your sincere friend Superintendent 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash. March 18, 1918 Mr. E. H. Hammond, Supt. Cushman School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mr. Hammond: Peter Dan, one of the Indian judges and father of Patsy Moses, requests me to write you asking that you permit Patsy to return on April 1 for the purpose of assisting in the spring work. Peter is a [blacked-out] blood and one of the energetic Indians who is setting a good example for all others. He contemplates seeding to spring grain about 100 acres. His health is not good and he must depend on his two boys, one of whom is living at home. I respectfully recommend that his application be given favorable consideration. Very respectfully, Fred C. Gov. R. W. for Lands DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash December 10, 1917 Mr. E. H. Hammond, Supt. Cushman School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Sir: Peter Dan, father of Patsy Moses, has been in the office several times lately in the interest of his son, whom it appears is in a logging camp on the Coast. Peter was determined that I should send Patsy sufficient funds to pay his transportation back to the reservation. I refused to do this until I ascertained from you whether or not you were going to get this boy. If you do not care to have him return to your school please advise at the earliest possible date and I will endeavor to send him money to return home on. His father is one of the Indian judges and a splendid man. He is very much worried because his son left school and is in a logging camp and living under what Peter thinks unfavorable conditions. I do not desire to appear unduly anxious in this matter but Peter has made several trips to the office and is very much worried. He showed me a letter today which Patsy had written him. It appears from his letter that there are many Indians living in the vicinity of this logging camp. This being the case I assume it would be rather hard to catch him if he endeavored to hide away as doubtless he would find assistance among his newmade friends. As a matter of discipline I should like to see Patsy returned to the school although he has declared in former letters to his father that he will not stay if returned. Please let me know what you desire to do in this matter in order that I may advise the father. Very respectfully, Fred C. DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash., May 15, 1916. Mr. T. B. Wilson, Supt. Cushman School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mr. Wilson: The father of Patsy Moses informs me that Patsy has been out of school for three weeks on account of ill health and the father is anxious for the boy to come home as soon as possible. For his travelling expenses I am enclosing a check on his account, No. 439, for $25.00. Very respectfully, [signature] J.M. Johnson Superintendent. VV Enc.-1 Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash., May 22, 1916. Mr. J. M. Johnson, Supt. Colville Agency, Nespelem, Washington. Dear Sir: I am in receipt of your letter of May 15th in regard to sending Patsie Moses home. I wish to state that Patsie is not sick but is attending school regularly. About a month ago he had a case of indigestion and he was sent to the hospital where he was given proper treatment. He was out in a few days. Later on he had a slight attack of rheumatism, and again he was sent to the hospital for treatment. The fact that a pupil is in the hospital is no evidence that they are seriously ill, because just as soon as a pupil complains of being sick, he is at once sent to the hospital for treatment, and frequently they are out in a few days. I wish to assure you and Patsie's father that Patsie's health is not such as it will require him to return home at this time. It is about a month until school closes and he will be sent home at that time. Very respectfully, Superintendent. TBW(S) Money for Patsy Moses. DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wn. February 18, 1916. Mr. T. B. Wilson, Superintendent, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Sir: Replying to your letter of January 28th in which you transmit the request of Patsy Moses for $25.00, I have to advise that I saw his father yesterday and told him that Patsy wanted money, and he said he would send some at once. Very respectfully, [signature] J. M. Johnson Superintendent. VV/B Wilbur, Wash. Nov. 22, 1917. Nite Letter E. H. Hammond Patsy Moses, Cosmopolis, working with section gang. His father anxious and will get him if you don't. Wire action taken. Morgan. Received. 8:35 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington. Nov. 14, 1917. The City Marshall, Cosmopolis, Washington. Dear Sir: I have received word that Paul Smitkin, a Colville Indian employed in a box factory at Cosmopolis was harboring three runaway boys from Cushman Trades School. If these boys are Stephen Raymond, Patsy Moses, Henry Polk or Victor Johnnelly they are deserters from this school. Please arrest them and advise me by wire and I will send for them immediately. Very respectfully, [signature] Superintendent. EHH - F Paul Smitkin & Stephen Raymond & Patsy Moses was working here but they only worked a few days. They left here on the 5th of this month yours truly W.T. Younger City Marshal RECORD OF PUPIL IN SCHOOL Record of ____________________________ at { ____________________________ School. (Name.) The law provides: "That no part of this appropriation, or any other appropriation provided for herein except appropriations made pursuant to treaties, shall be used to educate children of less than one-fourth Indian blood whose parents are citizens of the United States and of the State wherein they live and where there are adequate free-school facilities provided and the facilities of the Indian schools are needed for pupils of more than one-fourth Indian blood." (Act of August 1, 1914.) EXTRACTS FROM SCHOOL RULES. If the facilities of a school are not needed as provided in the above paragraph, children showing any Indian blood, whose parents live on an Indian reservation, and who if debarred from Government schools could not obtain an education, may be enrolled in the day and boarding schools of their reservation; these children, however, may not be transferred to nonreservation schools without special permission from the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Before enrolling a pupil superintendents must satisfy themselves whether he has left any other school without permission and whether he has been expelled for cause from any other school. A pupil who has been expelled for cause from any Indian school may be reenrolled in any Indian school only with permission of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. "The Secretary of the Interior may in his discretion withhold rations, clothing, and other annuities from Indian parents or guardians who refuse to or neglect to send or keep their children of proper school age in some school during a reasonable portion of each year."
